wrong_text: an inert shielding gas (argon or CO₂) protects the molten pool from atmospheric contamination
problem: CO₂ is NOT an inert gas — it is an active gas that reacts with the weld pool. When CO₂ (or an argon/CO₂ mix) is used the process is technically MAG (Metal Active Gas) welding, not MIG. True MIG welding uses argon or argon/helium mixtures and is suited to non-ferrous metals. The GCSE-level description listing CO₂ as an 'inert' shielding gas is technically incorrect and will contradict exam mark schemes that ask students to distinguish MIG from MAG.
correction: Change to: 'an inert or active shielding gas (pure argon for non-ferrous metals; argon/CO₂ mix — technically MAG — for steel) protects the molten pool from atmospheric contamination. In practice the MIG/MAG distinction is often collapsed to just "MIG" in workshop usage, but for exam purposes argon is the inert shielding gas associated with MIG and CO₂ is an active gas used in MAG welding of steel.' For a GCSE-safe simplification, remove CO₂ from the parenthesis and write: 'an inert shielding gas (typically argon or an argon-rich mixture)'.

wrong_text: an inert shielding gas (argon or CO₂)
problem: Same issue reflected in the collapsible 'Welding, Brazing and Soldering at a Glance' section (n20) which correctly calls MIG a process that uses an 'inert' gas — but the earlier explicit bracketed example '(argon or CO₂)' will be memorised by students as fact. The inconsistency within the same lesson reinforces the error.
correction: Remove CO₂ from the bracket in n5. The collapsible section does not repeat the error independently, so only n5 needs changing.

problem: Minor range boundary issue. Most engineering sources place mild/low-carbon steel at 0.05–0.25% (or up to 0.30%). The lower bound of 0.1% is slightly high — 'dead mild' steel can be as low as 0.05%. The upper bound of 0.3% is at the very top edge of accepted ranges and overlaps with medium carbon steel. UK GCSE D&T materials routinely use '0.1–0.3%' as a simplified teaching range, so this is acceptable for the course level; however the same range is repeated verbatim in the Key Fact box and flashcards and may be penalised if a mark scheme uses 0.05–0.25% or ≤0.3%. Flag as LOW — acceptable for GCSE but worth noting.
correction: Consider widening to 'up to approximately 0.3% carbon' or using '0.05–0.3%' to be safe across mark schemes. The current value is within teaching convention for Eduqas D&T but is at the outer limit.
